name: Deep Slate-Olive
lede: Deep Slate-Olive is a greyed-down olive, the "deep" modifier of [[slate-olive]], listed on Ridgway's 1912 plate and in the 1955 ISCC-NBS system.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body:
The name follows the library's modifier grammar, *deep* plus [[slate-olive]], the base color [1]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XLVII, hue 29′′′′, tone k, placed the original hue, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 later filed this chip into block 156, named dark greenish gray in that system's own list [1]. No further origin for the base name "slate-olive" is recorded here.

Its nearest look-alikes on file are [[ebony]] and [[bronze-green]], both within about 3.5 units, with [[dusky-green]] close behind [2]. The hue sits in the Neutrals family: olive pulled toward grey rather than toward brown or blue [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 2.88% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (686 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 361 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 79% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 3.9% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (66 paintings), 2.5 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 34% of its 361 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Paul Cezanne, present in 8 of 50 works here, 5.7x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 5.0x) [3]. It is most over-represented in Norway, 3.2x expected (8 of 120 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1301, 611 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
